title: Reducing the Negative Grip of Gossip
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that gossip is a corrosive but nearly unavoidable feature of team life, one that thrives whenever leaders leave an information vacuum for people to fill with speculation. Rather than treating gossip as simply a discipline problem, the author frames it as a leadership-communication problem: transparency and proactive information-sharing are the real antidotes. The piece also introduces the idea of cultivating deliberate 'positive gossip' as a counterweight, so that sharing good news becomes the socially rewarded behavior instead of trading in rumors. It closes by tying the argument to the classic maxim distinguishing what great, average, and small minds discuss.
points: Transparency is the primary defense against gossip: when leaders keep teams well-informed, people have less need to speculate and invent explanations.
Deliberately cultivating a culture of 'positive gossip' — team members competing to share good news — crowds out negative rumor-sharing.
Gossip persists because it lets people air grievances about unpopular decisions safely, without anyone in authority to counter the narrative.
Frequent open forums where concerns can be raised directly reduce the fuel that feeds rumor and cynicism.
quotes: Gossip is the idle talk about people and events that can sometimes overpower a team or organization and create a toxic work climate.
Teams with a high occurrence of gossip experience lower productivity and poor morale.
With no one in authority to set the record straight or to make a counterargument, gossip allows people to air perceived grievances with safety.

Creating a culture of positive gossip, where team members are on the lookout for positive information to share with others, makes negative gossip stand out as pessimistic and unworthy of distribution.
Great minds discuss ideas; average minds discuss events; small minds discuss people.
